name: drg-0001-goal1
goal: Outline every neuron cell body and count them, leaving out the satellite glia and Schwann cells around them.

look.notes: The image is a fluorescence microscopy image of a rat dorsal root ganglion (DRG) section stained with an antibody against neurofilament. The bright spots represent neurons. The total number of neurons in the section cannot be accurately determined from the provided images due to the lack of a clear, countable field of view and the presence of overlapping structures. The pixel size information provided (0.95 µm) is for the whole section, but the actual resolution of the images is not sufficient to reliably count individual cells. The number 1.52 µm per shown pixel in image 1 is likely a misinterpretation of the pixel size, as it is not consistent with the stated 0.95 µm per pixel. The actual number of neurons in a DRG section can vary widely, but it is typically in the range of tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands, not the extremely high number suggested by the calculation based on the provided pixel size and image dimensions. The provided number is not a reliable estimate of the neuron count.

steps.why: To identify all cell bodies that are likely neurons based on their size and morphology, which are typically larger and more distinct than satellite glia or Schwann cells.
To separate the identified cell bodies into those that are positive for neurofilament (neurons) and those that are negative (likely satellite glia or Schwann cells).
To count the number of neurons in the section after excluding satellite glia and Schwann cells.

plan.result: The analysis will outline and count the neuron cell bodies in the rat dorsal root ganglion section, excluding satellite glia and Schwann cells. The result will be an accurate count of neurons in the section.
risks: The resolution of the image may not be sufficient to clearly distinguish between neuron cell bodies and satellite glia or Schwann cells, leading to misclassification.
The staining may not be uniform, leading to some neurons being missed or incorrectly identified.
The segmentation may not be perfect, leading to over- or under-counting of neurons.
